name: Vitamin D / UVB for tan

card.summary: The overlap between sun-for-vitamin-D and sun-for-a-tan: UVB does both, but they are separate goals.
card.note: UV exposure raises sunburn and skin cancer risk; vitamin D can also come from diet or supplements.

quick.overview:
UVB radiation in sunlight both stimulates new melanin (tanning) and drives vitamin D production in skin. Some people cite vitamin D as a reason for sun or sunbed exposure that also gives them a tan.

Small registered trials have measured vitamin D after sunbed or UVB exposure, but this article does not rely on their results.
quick.mechanism: UVB converts a skin precursor into vitamin D3.[1] Melanin absorbs UV and inhibits UVB-driven vitamin D synthesis, which is why darker skin makes less for the same exposure.[1] UVB also stimulates new melanin, producing a tan that appears two to three days later.[2]
quick.risks: Excess UV is linked to sunburn, skin aging, DNA damage and skin cancer.[2] Wikipedia notes vitamin D can also come from diet and supplements, and health bodies publish intake guidance.[1]

lead: Vitamin D / UVB for tan refers to the overlap between exposing skin to ultraviolet B radiation for vitamin D production and doing so to obtain a tan. UVB converts a precursor in the skin into vitamin D3, which for most people supplies more vitamin D than diet.[1]
The same UVB band prompts melanocytes to make new melanin, which appears a few days after exposure.[2] Melanin in turn absorbs UV and reduces UVB-driven vitamin D synthesis.[1]

Several small trials of UVB, sunbeds and supplementation have been registered; this article describes their topics only. Public health bodies set intake recommendations for vitamin D that do not depend on tanning.[1]

paras: UVB in sunlight converts a precursor in the epidermis into cholecalciferol.[1] Melanin protects against UV damage but inhibits UVB-driven synthesis, and factors such as latitude, season, covering clothing and sunscreen reduce production.[1] Tanning follows from UVA oxidising existing melanin and UVB triggering new melanin, with the latter appearing in two to three days.[2]

Wikipedia reports a US recommended dietary allowance of 600 IU/day for ages 1 to 70, and UK NHS advice that at-risk people consider year-round supplements.[1] These recommendations do not call for tanning.[1]

Registered trials have examined related questions: vitamin D levels achieved by sunbed tanning in 87 healthy participants (started 2014),[3] 25-hydroxyvitamin D with and without supplementation in Caucasian women (started 2009),[4] and UVB light with sunscreen and vitamin D status in 50 people (started 2008).[5] Registrations also exist for vitamin D in cystic fibrosis[6] and chronic pancreatitis.[7] This article does not summarise their results. Wikipedia states that UV exposure alone can raise serum 25(OH)D to slightly above 100 nmol/L without reaching toxic levels.[1]

UV exposure is associated with sunburn, accelerated skin aging, DNA damage, immune impairment and increased skin cancer risk, and a 2010 study linked frequent tanning bed use to about triple the melanoma risk.[2]
